doc.title: Josephine Davies interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 14, 2025

title: Discovering jazz at Guildhall through Coltrane's 'A Love Supreme'
summary: A pop-listening teenager who entered Guildhall as a classical saxophonist, she heard 'A Love Supreme' in the halls and switched to the jazz course.

venues.name: Guildhall School of Music and Drama

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: A couple of things to wrap up with. I know it’s hard to pinpoint one thing ever, you know one thing. But is there one recording that you can point to that you heard perhaps in your teen years that just like opened your ears up and provided some inspiration to you?

Yes. I can very much pinpoint the album, because funnily enough I was not into jazz at all. I don’t think I ever heard any jazz as a teenager, or if I did I would have thought what is all this nonsense. You know I was listening to pretty much ‘80s pop music and ‘90s pop music. And I was into – maybe I won’t say that, it’s slightly embarrassing. But yes, some low profile popular music let’s say all through my teenage years. And I went to Guildhall, which is one of the music colleges in London, when I was 18, as a classical saxophonist and not really having thought about wanting to do music. I’d actually wanted to go into acting and then my best friend who is an opera singer was going to Guildhall and I just sort of followed her. I just had no sense of autonomy really when I was 17, 18 – I just kind of did what other people suggested which surprises me looking back. Anyway I got there and I was amazed that I got in actually because I was an incredibly average saxophonist. I just played a little bit. I think I passed like grade 8 or something quite recently, hadn’t really developed any sense of theory or aural or harmony skills, so really knew not very much at all. But I did get in and when I got there and they really showed me what classical alto actually sounds like I thought oh, I don’t really like this. Oh no, sort of oh what am I going to do, do I need to think about this. And in the halls of residence that I was living in in my first year someone had “A Love Supreme,” John Coltrane and I heard that and I thought well that sounds like freedom to me. That sounds like some kind of way of expressing life that would be affirming and useful and incredible. And then so I switched to the jazz course when I was 18 or 19 I should say.
We all have our albums, that’s for sure.
